content: This indicator is calculated by dividing the expenditure on program-specific operating costs by the GDP minus debt service, then multiplying by 100. It reflects the government's ability to pay for ongoing program costs. Data on GDP and debt service are typically accessible through ministries of finance and global databases. This indicator is calculated by dividing the expenditure on program-specific capital costs by the GDP minus debt service, then multiplying by 100. It reflects the government's ability to pay for capital investments. GDP and debt service data are readily available from ministries of finance and global databases. Loans obtained on a commercial basis to cover immunization and surveillance costs, such as specimen collection and laboratory testing, are considered national resources since the principal and interest must be repaid in full at commercial rates. Concessional loans, which are used to cover costs, are partially considered national resources and partially external, with the proportions determined by the grant component of the loan as estimated by the lender. When families face barriers to accessing immunization services due to a lack of information, a communications plan may be necessary to generate demand and improve coverage. Implementing a demand-generation plan, such as a communications strategy, can help address this issue. Countries applying for GAVI fund support are required to submit a financial plan as part of their multi-year strategic plan. This plan should include a five-year budget, identified financing sources, alignment with the strategic work plan and performance targets, commitments from development partners, and written approval from the Interagency Coordinating Committee (ICC). Non-fund-eligible countries may also adopt this approach. The financial plan should demonstrate the mobilization and efficient use of resources to achieve immunization program objectives. Efficient use of resources can be demonstrated by purchasing quality vaccines through global procurement mechanisms or direct procurement at prices within 10% of the global price for which the country is eligible. Specialized training in financing-related topics, complementary to other training such as vaccine management, is recommended to improve resource efficiency. Tracking vaccine wastage, particularly for expensive vaccines like hepatitis B or combination vaccines, is important due to the financial implications. Monitoring trends in vaccine stockouts by region and analyzing dropout rates between different vaccine doses (e.g., DTP1 to DTP3) can provide insights into program performance. Countries should conduct regular reviews of immunization policies, engage stakeholders such as NGOs, CSOs, and private sector leaders, and establish advisory groups like the National Immunization Technical Advisory Group (NITAG) to provide recommendations on policy reforms and new vaccine introductions. Annual and quarterly planning reviews, as well as monitoring and evaluation frameworks, should be implemented to track progress and improve program performance. Efforts to strengthen routine immunization should include identifying high-risk districts, conducting micro-planning workshops, and ensuring adequate cold-chain equipment and vaccine management systems. Achieving high coverage rates, such as 95% for DTP3 by 2018, requires collaboration with local authorities and the establishment of national databases for district indicators. Demand generation for immunization can be enhanced through knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) studies, incorporating lessons learned into policy and practice, and developing communication plans with key messages on routine immunization. Engaging professional associations and conducting regular press conferences can further support these efforts. Cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness analyses are essential tools for evaluating health programs. Cost-benefit analysis compares all costs and benefits of different interventions in monetary terms, while cost-effectiveness analysis identifies the least expensive way to achieve a specific objective, such as the number of lives saved or children vaccinated. Costing involves determining the total cost of a program over a year, with indicators like cost per capita, cost per dose, and cost per DTP3 child providing insights into program affordability and efficiency. Financial sustainability refers to a country's ability to mobilize and efficiently use domestic and external resources to achieve immunization targets reliably. A financial sustainability plan (FSP) outlines strategies to address financing challenges and support mediumand long-term program objectives. Baseline data provide a starting point for measuring changes, while benchmarks and targets help assess progress. Regular monitoring, evaluation, and feedback are critical for improving program performance and achieving objectives. Leadership and governance in immunization programs involve strategic policy frameworks, effective oversight, coalition building, accountability, and attention to system design. Strengthening health systems and ensuring adequate human resource management are essential for achieving immunization goals and improving overall program effectiveness.
